Subject: Post-call: fast-start burst charter & queueing handoff

Hi Samira / Ben —

Thanks for a productive call today. Quick recap plus the handoff items we discussed so your engineering and ops teams have something concrete to review. I captured the performance targets you confirmed and a proposed burst/warmpool approach for a fast-start pilot.

Recap (what Kaledon requested)
- Latency SLOs: 95th percentile <= 75ms for short text completions (~<200 tokens), 99th percentile <= 150ms for standard requests. Streaming-first-byte target <= 200ms for audio/transcription-style flows.
- Throughput/Concurrency: average steady-state concurrency ~200 concurrent calls; expected burst to peaks of ~1,800 concurrent calls for 5–20 minutes during morning batches.
- Availability: target 99.9% application-level availability during business hours.

Proposed Redwood fast-start charter (initial pilot)
- Warm pool: provision 30 prewarmed instances (model pinned to m-1.2q) to cover 200 concurrent baseline and absorb the first wave of traffic.
- Burst path: allow autoscaling up to 2,000 concurrent by spinning up additional instances (cold path) with queueing threshold at 85% instance utilization.
- Scale-up time expectations: prewarmed instances activate <5s; cold-start instance provisioning expected 45–90s depending on instance type and region.
- Priming behavior: once instances are live, KV-cache priming to reach steady throughput is expected to take ~60–90s per instance (depends on prompt prefix and avg seq length).
- Queueing behavior: requests are queued when available concurrency is exhausted; queueing strategy is FIFO with a 30s max wait before soft-fallback to a lower-cost smaller variant (m-1.2q -> m-1.1q) for non-critical flows.

Open questions / actions for Kaledon
1) Confirm the 99th/95th latency targets above are acceptable for the pilot.
2) Are there specific endpoints that must never be degraded (no soft-fallback)? If so, list them for hard route pinning.
3) Confirm whether warm pool instances should be regional (us-west) only, or split across two regions for redundancy.

Next steps (internal and external)
- Alex: share this recap + ask our infra team for measured scale-up and priming metrics (ETA: 24–36 hours).
- Karthik: provide a short engineering note with empirical cold/warm start numbers and queueing thresholds we use in similar pilots.
- Monica: schedule a 45-minute technical demo with Kaledon ops to walk the warm pool behavior and routing failover (T+3 business days).

Attachments referenced: none in this message — technical pack to follow from engineering.

Thanks —
Alex

2) Priming time: the 60–90s to hit steady throughput is acceptable, but what happens during that priming window if we get a sudden additional surge? Do we route to cold-start instances or queue?

Assuming answers above are reasonable, we are ready to move to a short pilot. Please include those empirical numbers and the demo invite.

Alex / team / Samira —

Short engineering readout (empirical and recommended defaults for the pilot). Numbers below are based on recent pilots with similar LLM footprints and medium-sequence workloads (~150 tokens avg). I attached the warmpool checklist and a small CSV with metric traces from a recent 1.5k-concurrency burst test.

Empirical numbers (typical cluster: 8-GPU pool, pinned model variant m-1.2q):
- Prewarmed activation: instances already in the warm pool return to ready in <5s (connection and health checks) — this covers immediate absorb for first ~30% of a sudden spike.
- Cold-start provisioning: new instances from the cold path (spin up + runtime init + model load) typically finish in 50–85s. Variability depends on region and available spare capacity.
- KV-cache priming: after model load the instance needs ~60–120s of sustained traffic to reach steady-state KV hit ratios; short bursts may see ~10–20% higher per-token latency during this period.
- Streaming-first-byte: under primed/warm conditions we meet <=200ms for ~96% of requests at up to 1,500 concurrent streaming connections. At >1,500 concurrent streaming flows, meet-rate drops toward 90% as network and tokenization hotspots appear. We can tune for higher percentiles with additional warm capacity.

Queueing & fallback behavior (recommended defaults)
- Queue threshold: begin queueing incoming requests when effective concurrency reaches 85% of combined warm + active live instances to avoid cascading cold starts.
- Max queue hold: 30s by default. If a request is still waiting after 30s, apply soft-fallback to smaller variant (m-1.1q) for non-critical endpoints; for endpoints marked critical, keep in queue until a slot frees for up to 90s then return 503 if not satisfied.
- Routing priority: critical endpoints (e.g., PHI-sensitive inference) should be hard-pinned to warm instances — no soft-fallback. We recommend Kaledon identify up to 10 endpoints as critical for the pilot.

Cost delta guidance (rough back-of-envelope)
- Keeping 30 prewarmed instances 24/7 increases baseline infra spend by ~24–28% vs spinning the same capacity up during business hours only (assumes on-demand GPU pricing and us-west region).
- Business-hours-only warm pool (8am–6pm local): cost drops ~35% vs 24/7, but you accept slower absorption for overnight/early-morning surprise bursts that arrive outside the warm window.

Pilot recommendation (safe default)
- Start with 30 prewarmed instances during business hours only (8am–6pm), add an additional 10 small prewarmed instances 24/7 for critical endpoints.
- Queue threshold: 85%; Max queue hold: 30s; Soft-fallback enabled for non-critical endpoints.
- Acceptance criteria: during a synthetic 2x baseline burst (target 1.8k concurrency) pilot must keep 95th latency below 150ms for short requests and meet streaming-first-byte <=200ms for >=95% of requests.

Attachments:
- warmpool-priming-checklist.pdf (checklist for priming, health checks, and observability hooks)
- burst-metrics.csv (metric traces from a 1.5k burst run)

I'll join the demo to walk through these items and show traces.
